**Proof.**  
Let \(m\ge 1\).  Take the “falling factorial’’ of length \(m\)

\[
f(x)= (x)_m = x(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-m+1).
\]

* The polynomial \(f\) has integer coefficients; its leading coefficient is \(1\),
  hence \(\gcd(a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_m)=1\) (i.e. it is primitive).

* For any positive integer \(k\),

  - if \(k<m\) then one factor of the product is \(k-(k)=0\), so \(f(k)=0\);
  - if \(k\ge m\) then  

    \[
    f(k)=\frac{k!}{(k-m)!}=m!\binom{k}{m},
    \]

    which is a multiple of \(m!\).

  Consequently \(f(k)\) is always divisible by \(m!\).  Since \(m\mid m!\), we have
  \(m\mid f(k)\) for every positive integer \(k\).

Thus the polynomial \(f(x)=(x)_m\) satisfies all the required conditions.  Because
\(m\) was arbitrary, **every** positive integer \(m\) can be realized.

\[
